newsitem.title: FRANCE: Parliament completes waste exports second reading.
newsitem.headline: Parliament completes waste exports second reading.

text.p: The European Parliament adopted on Wednesday its report on proposed amendments to a 1993 Council regulation on the export of hazardous waste.
The vote, a second reading under the cooperation procedure, concluded the Parliament's second visit to the Commission's original proposal, COM(95)143, of April 1995.
Euro-MPs adopted the four proposed amendments, reinserting elements from their first reading which the Council of Ministers had subsequently removed.

The main issue for deputies is the legal treatment of waste listed on the hazardous waste list in Council Decision 94/904/EC but which is not listed in proposed amendments to Regulation 259/93/EEC's various annexes. This excluded waste is defined in a proposed annex IIa, additional to the green list of wastes in the Regulation's annex II.
Annex III, the so-called amber waste list, details wastes which can be considered hazardous while annex IV, the red list, details those which are always hazardous.

Parties to the Basle Convention on the export of hazardous wastes have decided that from January 1, 1998, hazardous materials destined for recycling may no longer be exported by OECD countries to their non-OECD partners. This concerns annex III and IV wastes.
Rapporteur Ivar Virgin, a Swedish Christian Democrat, sought to have wastes which could be hazardous but which nevertheless fell outside these two annexes included in the pending export ban.
"The reason is that annex II contains waste categories which are not always without danger, and parliament wanted to close the loophole offered by annex II," Virgin said in his report.
The wastes in question mainly concern contaminated metal scrap.

Virgin said that there was no guarantee of environmentally sound use of such waste in importing countries and added that EU waste treatment principles of prevention, proximity of destruction or reuse were more important than the provision of cheap but contaminated materials to third countries.
European Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard reminded Euro-MPs during Tuesday's debate that Council had rejected just these amendments first time around.
